Selling a house in Detroit

Detroit is the seat of Wayne County and the largest city in Michigan. The 2025 estimate counts 649,095 residents, up from 639,111 in 2020. The county records your deed and holds older delinquent tax accounts, so many sale questions end at a county office rather than at city hall.

A house in Boston-Edison or Indian Village competes in a different market from a modest bungalow elsewhere in the city, even though both pay the same city and county taxes. Price your house against its own block, not against the city as a whole.

Detroit housing figures

Close to half of Detroit households rent, so investors and landlords are a real part of the buyer pool.

A typical owned home at $83,900 beside a typical rent of $1,074 means a rented house can repay its price quickly, which is why investors follow Detroit sales. The same gap makes a roof or furnace replacement a heavy share of a sale price here.

Older houses and what inspectors flag

Beyond downtown and New Center, Detroit is mostly low-rise. Working-class areas built before World War II have wood-frame and brick houses, while Brush Park, Woodbridge, Indian Village, Palmer Woods and Boston-Edison have larger, more ornate homes.

Older houses on clay soil tend to draw the same inspection comments:

  • Furnaces, roofs and plumbing, because the winters are hard on them.
  • Cooling and attic ventilation for the hot weeks.
  • Basement moisture and drainage, since clay holds water against foundations.

Fix these items or price them in before you list.

Who buys and what helps a listing

Midtown's Detroit Medical Center employs more people than anyone else in the city, with Wayne State University beside it and the Henry Ford Health System in New Center. Roughly 80,500 people work downtown, one-fifth of the city's jobs, and buyers who work in those districts look for housing nearby.

Getting around is easier than in many Michigan cities. DDOT buses, the QLINE streetcar and the downtown People Mover loop serve the core, and SMART runs routes to the suburbs. Many families also look at suburban school districts, so ask your agent how school boundaries affect the buyer pool on your street.

State deed tax and filings

Michigan puts its deed tax on the seller. Every $500 block of value carries $3.75 of state tax, and a county layer sits on top: 55 cents per block in a county under two million residents. MCL 207.523, 207.525 and 207.504 set the framework, and the Wayne County deed office confirms the current county rate. You have 15 days from handing over the deed to pay the county treasurer.

MCL 207.526 exempts certain deeds, including a court-ordered transfer with no stated price, a foreclosure deed, and an instrument that creates a joint tenancy where one of the owners already held the property. A lender that later resells a foreclosed house does not get the same break.

  • The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor inside 45 days (MCL 211.27a).
  • For the next calendar year, taxable value is set at the SEV.
  • Ask the Detroit assessor for the form that ends your own principal residence exemption.

For current-year and past-due bill amounts, ask the City of Detroit Office of the Assessor and the Wayne County Treasurer for written payoff figures before you sign anything.

Selling before a tax foreclosure auction

The Wayne County Treasurer, whose office is at 400 Monroe Street in Detroit, holds an annual online auction of tax-foreclosed properties. The minimum bid is a fixed amount that includes the treasurer's foreclosure and auction costs. Winners have 72 hours to pay in full, and the office records a quit claim deed within 30 days after the auction closes.

Selling before the auction lets you choose the buyer and the price. Call the treasurer and ask what redemption rights remain on your parcel and whether a payment plan is available. Have the closing agent settle any balance from your proceeds, since a buyer's lender expects the lien cleared when the deed changes hands.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Detroit houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Comparing offers on a house that needs work

Three questions decide most Detroit sales: what an appraiser will accept, what an inspector will list, and what taxes are still open on the parcel. A mortgage buyer needs all three to line up. An investor offer skips the appraisal, and an as-is contract can say who clears trash, personal property and open utility accounts.

Line up offers by what you walk away with: price, minus deed tax, minus unpaid taxes and liens, minus repairs you would otherwise fund. Ask each bidder for evidence of funds and a dated closing plan before you choose.

A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and most repair requests, which matters when the house has a worn roof, old plumbing or damp basement. Whatever route you pick, gather the payoff letters first so nothing about the liens surprises you after you sign.

What to gather before you list

Put together your deed information, recent tax bills and a note of any open utility accounts. If the house is a rental, ask the City of Detroit what compliance rules apply to your property type and whether anything is outstanding. Request written payoff figures from the City of Detroit Office of the Assessor and the Wayne County Treasurer. With those papers in hand, a buyer or closing agent can move quickly, and you can compare offers on real numbers instead of guesses.

What happens at a Detroit closing

The closing agent reads the payoff letters, subtracts the deed tax and any liens from the price, and sends you the remainder. The deed is recorded with Wayne County, and the buyer then reports the transfer to the assessor. If you had a principal residence exemption, file the form that ends it so the new owner's bill is set correctly.

Walk through the house before closing and clear out trash and personal property, since an as-is contract usually makes that the seller's job. Settle open utility accounts on the day you hand over the keys. A sale where the buyer pays cash and accepts the house as it is tends to close with fewer of these loose ends, because no lender is waiting on an appraisal or a repair list.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Which side owes the state deed tax on a Detroit house?

The seller. Michigan names the grantor as the liable party. The state takes $3.75 on each $500 block, Wayne County adds its portion, and a court-ordered transfer without a stated price is among the exempt deeds.

Can a Detroit house with unpaid taxes still be sold?

Yes. Request an official payoff letter from the Wayne County Treasurer and let the closing agent settle it out of your proceeds. Selling ahead of the county's foreclosure auction keeps the choice of buyer with you.

How does a sale change the Detroit tax bill?

The buyer's taxable value is reset for the next year to the SEV, the figure the assessor sets at half of market value. The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor inside 45 days.

Must I repair my Detroit house before selling?

Buyers and their lenders often ask for repairs, and the contract decides who pays. Ask the City of Detroit about any compliance rules that apply to your property type, especially a rental.

How many people live in Detroit, and what do homes sell for?

The 2025 estimate counts 649,095 residents. For 2020 to 2024 the middle price of an owned house is $83,900, and about one home in two has its owner living inside.

What sets the pace of a Grand Rapids sale

Pace here follows the neighborhood, the condition of the house and whether a landlord or an owner-occupant holds title. Grand Rapids is the Kent County seat and Michigan's second most populated municipality, with 198,917 residents in 2020 and an estimated 201,183 in 2025. It is the economic center of West Michigan, and a metro area of about 1.2 million people feeds demand for housing.

An owner can hire an agent, sell directly to another party, or accept a cash purchase of the house as it stands. Each path runs through the city's rental rules, neighborhoods and tax process in its own way.

Grand Rapids housing figures

Health care, food, manufacturing and education jobs support steady demand, and the city's population grew 1.2% from April 2020 to July 2025. Owners and renters split almost evenly, and the middle owner-occupied home is valued at $244,500.

Grand Rapids housing and households, recent survey years unless noted
Housing measureGrand Rapids figure
Growth since April 2020+1.2%
Households that own their home54.0%
Typical price of an owner's house$244,500
Typical monthly rent$1,266
Occupied households80,222
Average trip to work19.0 minutes

The 19-minute average trip to work is worth mentioning when you describe the house, since the Medical Mile, downtown and the freeways are all close.

Neighborhoods and roads

The city lists 37 distinct neighborhoods, among them Heritage Hill, Eastown, East Hills, Alger Heights, Creston, Garfield Park, Midtown, Belknap Lookout, Roosevelt Park and the North End. Mailing addresses are divided into NE, NW, SE and SW quadrants, with Fulton Street as the north-south dividing line and Division Avenue as the east-west one, so check the quadrant in any address you quote.

Highways shape commute choices. I-96 runs along the north and northeast sides, I-196 crosses east to west, US 131 runs north to south, and M-6 loops the south side. The Rapid operates the buses, and DASH shuttles are free downtown.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Grand Rapids house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Rental certificates and vacant registration

The city requires a Certificate of Compliance before anyone lives in a rental unit. Owners register rental properties every year, and registration is free. Vacant properties must be registered within 15 days of becoming vacant. Certificates run two, four or six years depending on the property, and the city sends a reminder 90 days before recertification.

A rental inspection can end three ways. With no violations, the owner receives a certificate. With minor violations, the inspector gives verbal orders with a 14-day repair deadline. With major violations, a Notice of Violation sets a deadline of 60 or 120 days. Tenants should get 48 hours of notice before an inspection. Call Code Compliance at 616-456-3053 to check an address.

  • A landlord with a certified rental can hand the buyer a clean compliance record.
  • A rental that is vacant needs a vacant-property registration.
  • Rentals that use fuel-burning equipment must pass a mechanical safety inspection as part of certification.

Accessory units and short-term rentals

These rules matter if the property has a second unit. The zoning ordinance allows accessory dwelling units on single and two-family lots, up to 1,000 square feet and never larger than the main house. An accessory unit cannot be rented for fewer than 30 days, so Airbnb and Vrbo style use is not allowed, and a leased unit must be registered and certified as a rental. A deed restriction must be recorded so the unit is not conveyed separately from the house.

If your property has a second unit or a rented room, ask the Planning Department at planning@grcity.us before you list so the paperwork matches what you advertise.

Winter and your listing

Lake Michigan lies about 25 miles west, and lake-effect storms can arrive suddenly. Winters are cold and snowy, and buyers walking through in January notice drafts, ice dams and cold basements. Roofs, gutters, furnaces and basement moisture draw close attention from buyers in that climate. A seller who lists in winter should have the furnace serviced and the roof checked first.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Grand Rapids houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfer tax and filings

Michigan's county tax of 55 cents and state tax of $3.75 on each $500 of price are the seller's to pay (MCL 207.504 and 207.525), and the Kent County treasurer collects within 15 days after the deed is delivered (MCL 207.523). The settlement statement shows the exact figure.

The buyer notifies the assessor within 45 days so taxable value can reset to the state equalized value the next calendar year (MCL 211.27a). A higher bill for the buyer is a common talking point in negotiation, so be ready to explain it.

When an as-is sale beats a listing

Strong buyer demand favors a traditional listing for a house in good repair. An as-is sale fits deferred maintenance, an estate, tenant trouble or a firm moving date.

  • A listing fits an updated house when you can allow time for showings and financing.
  • An as-is buyer fits a vacant house, one with open code orders, or one that needs work before a lender would approve a loan.
  • Another landlord may pay more for a property that already holds a current Certificate of Compliance.

Ask for proof of funds, weigh offers by net proceeds, and put the closing date in writing. Cash buyers usually skip the appraisal and lender repair demands, which can shave weeks off the timeline when a house has open code orders or needs a new roof.

Before you list: a short to-do list

If the house is rented, call Code Compliance and ask where the Certificate of Compliance stands, then gather the certificate and any inspection orders for the buyer. If it is empty, register it as vacant and keep that record. If there is a second unit, confirm with the Planning Department that it matches the zoning rules.

Next, confirm the quadrant and neighborhood in your listing address. Buyers search by neighborhood first, so name it in the first line of the listing, and a wrong quadrant sends them to the wrong part of town. Gather your last tax bill and any recent repair receipts as well, since buyers like to see what has been replaced. Finally, ask your closing agent about the tax proration and the exact transfer tax so you know what you keep. If the house has tenants, tell buyers early whether the lease continues or ends at closing. A house that arrives with its papers in order tends to close without surprises, whichever route you choose.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does a rented Grand Rapids house need a compliance certificate?

Yes. The city requires a Certificate of Compliance before anyone lives in a rental unit, so a rented house should hold a current one. Call Code Compliance at 616-456-3053 to check an address.

Must I register an empty house in Grand Rapids?

Yes. Vacant properties must be registered within 15 days of becoming vacant, and registration is free. You can register online, by mail or at the Code Compliance office on Monroe Avenue NW.

Is an accessory unit allowed as a short-term rental?

No. The city bars accessory units from rentals under 30 days, and a leased unit must be registered and certified through Code Compliance.

Who pays the Michigan transfer tax on a Grand Rapids sale?

The seller. It is 55 cents per $500 for the county plus $3.75 per $500 for the state, and the settlement statement lists the exact amount.

Will a Grand Rapids buyer pay more in property tax than I do?

Usually. Taxable value resets to the state equalized value in the calendar year after the transfer, and the buyer must notify the assessor within 45 days.

Selling in Warren?

What a Warren homeowner should know before selling

Three local pieces shape a Warren sale: a few Building Division and rental rules, the Macomb County recording office in Mount Clemens, and a tax calendar that splits between city and county. Warren is Macomb County's biggest community and the state's third-largest city, so title agents and inspectors here run through these items all the time.

Accepting a cash offer on an as-is basis skips the showings and the repair list. It does nothing to the recording step, the seller's transfer tax, or any city bill still attached to the parcel. The headings below follow the order in which a seller usually runs into each one.

The Warren housing market

Warren occupies a six-by-six mile square at the southwest tip of Macomb County, between 8 Mile Road and 14 Mile Road, and it wraps around the small city of Center Line. The entire southern edge touches Detroit. Southeast Warren has many bungalows from the years right after World War II, and north of Stephens Road a lot of the housing is brick ranches from after 1960.

  • Southeast Warren takes in Warrendale, Belangers Garden, Berkshire Manor and Piper Van Dyke.
  • Southwest Warren holds Fitzgerald and Beierman Farms.
  • Northeast Warren includes Bear Creek, Bella Vista Estates, Fairlane Estates and downtown.
  • Northwest Warren is mostly the west half of Warren Con.

Cold matters for a house of this age. Warren sees about 39 days a year when it never climbs above freezing, so a buyer's inspector will look hard at the furnace, roof and pipes.

I-696 runs east and west across the city, and Van Dyke Avenue (M-53) divides it north from south. Macomb Intermediate School District oversees the six public districts that serve Warren. District lines wind through neighborhoods, so check the district tied to a particular address instead of trusting a street name.

Home values and ownership

Warren's estimated population for July 1, 2025 is 137,138, which sits 1.6 percent below the April 2020 base. From 2020 through 2024 the city had 54,744 households of roughly 2.5 people, and 71.1 percent of them owned their home.

Owner-occupied homes have a median value of $193,400. Renters pay a median gross rent of $1,225, and the median household income is $64,016. Typical monthly owner costs are $1,403 for those with a mortgage and $557 for those without. A single block can look quite different from any of these citywide numbers.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Warren house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

City rules that affect a Warren sale

Warren's residential city certification covers a vacant dwelling that has been posted "no occupancy": nobody may move in until the Building Division confirms the house meets the International Property Maintenance Code and the zoning ordinance. The office is at One City Square, Suite 305 (586-574-4504).

Rental owners face more. The rental ordinance sets these terms:

  • No one may rent or occupy a rental dwelling without a rental license, and licenses do not transfer between landlords or units.
  • A license lasts two years and needs a biennial inspection.
  • Sale of the property ends the license immediately.
  • No license is issued until prior property taxes, special assessments, water or sewer bills and mowing or cleanup charges are paid.

If tenants live in the house, call the Rental Inspections Division at 586-574-4633 and find out where the license stands before you list. Open balances there are easy to miss.

The same Building Division enforces the Michigan Building Code and Michigan Residential Code, along with Warren's zoning ordinance. A sunroom, deck or finished basement built without a permit is the kind of item that surfaces during a buyer's walkthrough, so gather permit records for past work early.

Recording a Warren deed and the charges

Warren lies in Macomb County, so the deed is filed with the county Register of Deeds at 120 N. Main St. in Mount Clemens (phone 586-469-7953). Counter hours run weekdays from 8 a.m. until 4:15 p.m. A flat per-document fee has applied since October 1, 2016, whatever the page count.

Macomb County recording and transfer tax charges
ChargeAmount
Deed, mortgage or other instrument$30 per document
Document assigning or discharging several instruments$3 added for each extra instrument
Tax certificate (warranty deeds, land contracts)$5 for up to five legal descriptions
State transfer taxSale price multiplied by .0075
Macomb County transfer taxSale price multiplied by .0011

Before a warranty deed or land contract is accepted, it needs a tax certificate from the county treasurer. The seller carries the transfer tax. Macomb publishes a schedule in $500 steps for anyone who wants the exact figure for a price.

Due dates and penalties for Warren property taxes

The City of Warren sends summer bills (city and school) in early July and winter bills (county) in early December. The Treasurer's Office at 586-574-4542 can confirm the dates for the current year.

  • Pay the summer bill whole, or split it by paying the first half by August 31. The second half is billed December 1 and due January 31.
  • From September 1 only the entire summer balance is taken, with a 1 percent fee that month and half a percent for every month after.
  • The winter bill is payable December 1 through February 28.
  • A balance still open after February 28 goes to the Macomb County Treasurer, with a further 4 percent fee and 1 percent interest monthly.

Ask your title agent how these will be divided at closing. An unpaid bill can hold up a rental license or a clear title, so call the Treasurer's Office before you accept an offer.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Warren houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Steps for a quick Warren sale

First, find out whether the house carries a no-occupancy posting, and if it is rented, check the license. Second, call the Treasurer's Office to learn what is owed and when. Third, gather permit records for any deck, sunroom or basement work. Fourth, collect offers in writing and compare closing dates and who pays what. After you accept, the title company orders the tax certificate for a warranty deed, confirms the transfer tax and records the deed in Mount Clemens.

Bring a few things to the title company: a payoff letter if you have a mortgage, your latest tax bill, any rental license paperwork and permit records. Ask for a written closing statement before the signing, and check that the tax split and the recording charges match your contract. A cash buyer needs no lender appraisal, which removes one common delay, but the city and county steps above still apply.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need a city inspection to sell my Warren house?

The city certification covers vacant houses marked no occupancy, which must pass a Building Division inspection before anyone moves in. Phone 586-574-4504 to learn whether your parcel carries that posting.

What happens to a Warren rental license when the property sells?

It ends at once. Licenses cannot move between owners, so the new owner applies again and the unit is inspected afresh.

Who pays transfer tax when a Warren house sells?

The seller does. The state rate is .0075 times the sale price and the county rate is .0011 times the sale price, and both are collected at recording.

Which office records the deed on a Warren sale?

The Macomb County Register of Deeds in Mount Clemens. The fee is $30 for the document, and a warranty deed first needs a tax certificate from the county treasurer.

What if I am behind on Warren property taxes before a sale?

Pay the Warren Treasurer's Office before the winter bill's February 28 cutoff. After that the balance moves to the Macomb County Treasurer with added fees and monthly interest, so clear it or have the title agent include it in the payoff.

Which selling routes move fastest in Sterling Heights?

Owners here have three working routes. A broker can market the house, you can look for a buyer yourself, or an investor can buy it for cash. Brokered sales tend to pay the most, and investor purchases tend to close soonest.

A mortgage buyer adds steps. The lender orders an appraisal, an inspector writes a report, and either document can reopen a price you thought was settled. A cash buyer skips those steps, which appeals to owners of worn-out roofs and dated kitchens in the older subdivisions.

  • Brokered sale: biggest pool of buyers, a commission at closing, and weeks or months to the right offer.
  • Private sale: no commission, but contract, showings and deed are yours to arrange.
  • Cash purchase: the buyer accepts the property as is, and the closing date is part of the deal.

Have each bidder write price, closing date, tax responsibility and inspection rights on one page, then compare what reaches you after payoff and costs.

The Sterling Heights market

The city covers about 36 square miles of Macomb County, a second-ring suburb well north of the Detroit core. Warren is its southern neighbor, Troy sits across the western line, Utica and Shelby Township lie north, and Clinton Township lies east. Most of the housing went up when auto-industry jobs filled the subdivisions in the 1960s and 1970s, and residents voted to incorporate in 1968.

There are 133,931 residents as of July 2025, against 134,346 in 2020, and 51,736 households. The typical owner-occupied home is worth $274,300, and 75.8% of homes are lived in by their owners, so the people touring your house are mostly future neighbors. Days that never climb above freezing number about 39 a year, which is why buyers ask about furnaces and roofs. Over a third of residents (35.2%) use another language at home, so clear photos and plain written terms help a sale.

Use these as a sanity check against your own list price, and ask your agent or buyer which recent sales on your street sit closest to your house.

School districts and main roads

Utica Community Schools covers the northern half of Sterling Heights, and Warren Consolidated Schools covers the southern half. Utica operates Stevenson High School and Henry Ford II High School here, while Warren Consolidated runs Sterling Heights High School. Parkway Christian School serves private-school families from kindergarten through twelfth grade.

The line runs through the middle of town, so similar houses a mile apart can feed different high schools. Name the district in your listing.

  • M-53 (Van Dyke) heads north toward the Thumb and south toward Detroit.
  • M-59 (Hall Road) links Macomb and Oakland counties and lines up the shopping district around Lakeside Mall.
  • Mound Road is the long north-south artery, and the numbered mile roads from 14 through 20 handle east-west trips. Sixteen Mile doubles as Metro Parkway.

Houses along these corridors sell on convenience. Streets farther in sell on lot size and schools.

Transfer tax on a Sterling Heights sale

The seller is liable, and the county treasurer expects payment within 15 days after the deed is delivered (MCL 207.523). The state tax runs $3.75 for each $500 of value, rounded up (MCL 207.525).

On the county's published schedule, the price is multiplied by .0075 for the state share and .0011 for the county share. The title agent's settlement statement shows the real total.

Some deeds are exempt under MCL 207.526, among them gifts to children and grandchildren and deeds in foreclosure. An exempt deed must quote the statute and lettered subsection.

Property taxes and the buyer's bill

The buyer's bill can come out well above yours. After a transfer, Taxable Value steps up to State Equalized Value, and the yearly cap on increases begins again from that level.

The Property Transfer Affidavit (Form 2766) is the buyer's job, due at Assessing in 45 days. A seller who claimed a Principal Residence Exemption files Form 2602 to end it. Owners who bought first and sell second can ask to keep the old exemption up to three years, provided the vacated house stays listed, unrented and free of business use.

  • Summer bill: arrives in late June, payable from July 1 into early September.
  • Winter bill: arrives in late November, payable from December 1 through February.
  • A summer balance left after Labor Day grows monthly, and an added 3% lands on March 1 as the account moves to the county.

Notices of assessment are mailed at the end of February, and a March Board of Review hears appeals. Reach Assessing at 586-446-2340 and the treasury at 586-446-2780.

The city treasury sits at 40555 Utica Road and is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and it keeps drop boxes on the city center campus for payments. Once a bill passes March 1, payment moves to the Macomb County Building at 1 South Main in Mount Clemens, phone 586-469-5190. Escrow agents receive the original bills, so a seller with an escrow account should confirm that the final bill was paid before the closing date.

Recording the deed in Macomb County

Recording takes place at the county Register of Deeds, 120 N. Main St., Mount Clemens, (586) 469-7953. Title agents usually deliver the deed, but private sellers should know what gets paper rejected.

  • Ink signatures in the original, each name printed below, and a notary block spelling every name identically.
  • Buyer addresses and the preparer's details on the deed itself.
  • A tall top margin on page one (2.5 inches) and narrow ones (half an inch) elsewhere.
  • A recorded, referenced death certificate if an owner has died.

A rejected deed pushes back the buyer's title, and your payout with it.

Comparing competing offers

Rank offers by net proceeds, speed and the odds of closing. A slightly higher bid with a long inspection window can lose to a modest cash bid with a fixed date.

Confirm who buys the title policy, whether leftover belongings stay, and whether the buyer may assign the contract to someone else. With a mortgage, get a written payoff letter first, since that balance comes off your proceeds.

Before you accept, ask each bidder for proof of funds or a lender letter, and put the deadline for removing any inspection condition in writing. Then book the title agent early, so the transfer tax, the tax proration and the deed recording are already lined up when the closing date arrives.

Frequently asked questions

Can a Sterling Heights house in poor shape still sell?

Yes. Some buyers will contract for it as is, and cash buyers do so most often. Financed buyers may ask for repairs once the appraisal arrives.

Who covers the transfer tax at a Sterling Heights closing?

The statute makes the seller liable, though your contract can say otherwise. Your settlement statement lists the state and Macomb County amounts.

Will taxes jump for whoever buys my house?

They can. The year after a transfer, Taxable Value resets to State Equalized Value. The buyer reports the purchase on the Property Transfer Affidavit.

Where does the Sterling Heights deed go after closing?

It is recorded with the Macomb County Register of Deeds. The office will return it if signatures, margins or notary details are off.

Which district will the buyer's children attend?

Utica Community Schools covers the north half of the city and Warren Consolidated Schools the south half. The street address decides.

The Ann Arbor housing market

Renters, graduate students and short stays drive much of this market, and prices sit far above state norms. Owning a typical home costs $2,436 a month with a mortgage, compared with a $1,649 median rent. Owners live in fewer than half of homes, so many houses here are rentals, and buyers will raise licensing early in a conversation.

About one resident in three had a different address a year earlier. That turnover keeps a steady flow of people looking for housing, which helps a seller who is ready to move.

What the University of Michigan means for a seller

It means a deep, stable pool of employed buyers and renters. The university employs about 30,000 people, roughly 12,000 of them at the medical center, and research money brings in technology firms, labs and startups. Auto firms such as General Motors and Visteon also employ residents.

Buyers check three things when they look at a house: how it connects to the freeways, whether it sits near parks, and which high school it feeds. US-23 hugs the east side, M-14 the north and I-94 the south and west. TheRide runs buses across the city and into Ypsilanti, and Amtrak's Wolverine stops at the Ann Arbor station. Ann Arbor Public Schools runs Pioneer, Huron, Skyline and Community high schools, so name the school zone in your listing.

Hills and drainage

The Huron River gives the city its hilly shape. Houses on the slopes have different drainage, views and basements than those on flat ground. Gather receipts for roof, gutter and drainage work before you list, and offer your repair records up front. A buyer's inspector will look hard at basement walls and sump pumps, and records answer those questions before they turn into price cuts.

If the house sits near the river or at the bottom of a slope, say what you know about water in the basement before the buyer asks. Photos of dry walls after a heavy rain, or a note about a past sump pump replacement, carry more weight than a general promise. A seller with a clear record usually gets fewer last-minute requests, and the sale moves along faster than it otherwise would.

Mature ash trees are another thing to check. Emerald ash borers have killed many of the city's roughly 10,500 ash trees, so look at any ash standing near your house or the sewer line.

Short-term rentals

A buyer can run a short-term rental in an Ann Arbor house only with a city license, and the zoning rules narrow who can get one. Chapter 97 of the city code covers stays of 30 consecutive days or fewer, and the license costs $500 per unit each year.

  • In zones whose names begin with R, only the owner's principal residence can qualify, backed by a sworn statement of principal residency.
  • Accessory dwelling units cannot be short-term rentals.
  • Companies acting for an owner cannot hold a license, and neither can a tenant who never moved in.
  • A non-owner-occupied property in a zone that permits one needs a valid Certificate of Compliance first.
  • Apply and pay through the city's STREAM portal. Review takes up to 21 business days, denied applications are not refunded, and the license renews yearly.

Some investors picture a vacation rental and then learn the zone forbids it. For long-term renting, the city runs a Green Rental Housing program with a HERS energy score of 110 or lower as its pass mark. If your house already operates as a rental, hand the buyer its paperwork.

Assessments, appeals and transfers

The Assessor's Office is on the fifth floor of Larcom City Hall, 301 E. Huron St. It takes the transfer affidavit and the exemption forms in person, by mail or through the city's online submission page, and answers at 734.794.6530. New owners file the Property Transfer Affidavit within 45 days, and sellers rescind their own principal residence exemption on the old home.

Why file promptly? Because the new owner's taxable value is recalculated from the transfer, and the assessor needs the affidavit to do it. The principal residence exemption comes off the old home when you rescind it, so do that on your side as soon as you have moved out. Both steps are simple forms, and the office will tell you what it needs if you call.

Property tax supplies more than half of city revenue. Taxable value moves each year by the inflation multiplier or 5 percent, whichever is lower, and a sale lifts it back toward assessed value. Notices go out in early March, and the Board of Review sits for four days beginning the Monday of the third week of March. A residential owner who is turned down there has until July 31 to go to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.

Deed recording and transfer tax

Washtenaw County has fewer than 2,000,000 residents, so the county tax is 55 cents per $500 and the state tax is $3.75 per $500. The seller pays at recording. State law sets the recording fee at $30 per document, but a charter county may set its own, so ask the Washtenaw County Register of Deeds for its table.

Warranty deeds need a county treasurer tax certificate. Exemptions cover transfers under $100, gifts from parent to child or grandparent to grandchild, and court-ordered transfers that set no price. If your sale qualifies, the deed has to say so.

Steps to sell an Ann Arbor house

  1. Decide whether the house is a rental, an owner-occupied home or a vacant property, since each draws different buyers and different paperwork.
  2. Collect repair receipts, any rental license or certificate, and your most recent tax statement.
  3. Ask the Assessor's Office at 734.794.6530 how to rescind your principal residence exemption.
  4. Have your closing agent confirm the treasurer's certificate for a warranty deed.
  5. Tell the buyer about the 45 day deadline for the Property Transfer Affidavit.

Timing matters. Notices go out in early March, so a house under contract in the spring may see a new assessment before closing. Ask your agent or closing attorney who is responsible if the tax bill changes between signing and the deed being recorded, and get the answer written into the purchase agreement.

A buyer paying cash can often skip the appraisal and inspection waiting that a mortgage buyer faces, but the transfer, tax and recording steps stay the same either way.

Frequently asked questions

Do owners or renters hold most Ann Arbor homes?

Renters hold the larger share. Owners occupy 45.5 percent of homes in the 2020 to 2024 figures.

How long does the short-term rental review take?

Up to 21 business days after the $500 payment. Applications go through the city's STREAM portal.

Who pays transfer tax on an Ann Arbor sale?

The seller pays it when the deed is recorded. The state charges $3.75 per $500 and the county charges 55 cents per $500.

Where do I file sale paperwork with the Ann Arbor assessor?

Larcom City Hall, fifth floor, 301 E. Huron St., or online. The office is reachable at 734.794.6530.

Can I appeal my Ann Arbor assessment?

Yes. The Board of Review sits for four days beginning the Monday of the third week of March. If it turns you down, a residential owner has until July 31 to go to the Michigan Tax Tribunal.

What is different about selling a house in Lansing?

As Michigan's capital, Lansing straddles three counties. Most parcels are in Ingham, some are in Eaton to the west, and some in Clinton to the north. That decides where your deed is recorded, so look at your tax bill first.

The July 2025 estimate is 113,884 residents, 1.1 percent more than the 2020 base. Homes here sell at a lower price level than most of suburban Michigan, and only a little over half are owner-occupied, so a good share of sellers are landlords.

Neighborhoods buyers recognize

The city is usually described in four sections, and buyers use the same names:

  • Eastside, east of the Grand River, centered on Michigan Avenue and the Frandor shopping center
  • Westside, around the river's curve, the most mixed by income and home type
  • Northwestside, the smallest section, near the Capital Region International Airport
  • Southside, the fourth section

Old Town, with buildings from the mid-1800s, and REO Town, along Washington Avenue, are the two historic districts people mention first. A listing that names its section and nearest corridor is easier for buyers to place.

Who buys houses in Lansing

Government, education, insurance and health care keep Lansing's job base broad, and state and university work means steady renters and first-time buyers. Investors also look for small, older houses. If your house is a rental, expect investor interest first. If it is owner-occupied and updated, the broader market may pay more.

Lansing School District covers most of the city, yet pieces fall into Holt, East Lansing, Okemos, Mason, Waverly, Grand Ledge and DeWitt, so confirm the district by address before you describe the school zone.

Lansing is crossed by I-96, I-69, I-496, US-127, M-43 along Saginaw Street and Grand River Avenue, and M-99 on Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard. Drivers reach Detroit or Grand Rapids in one highway run, which matters to buyers who commute or work for the state. A house within walking distance of a bus line or the river trail is worth naming in the listing text.

Prices, rents and repair costs

At that price level, one big repair bill takes a large bite out of a sale. Get two contractor quotes on any major item before you decide between listing and selling as-is.

Winters are cold, and snow averages 51.1 inches a season. For an older Lansing house, that points to the usual trouble spots: aging boilers and furnaces, thin attic insulation, frost-damaged porches and wet basements. Buyers pay attention to these items in any inspection report, so a clear service record helps in either a listing or a cash negotiation.

Do Lansing landlords have to register rentals before selling?

Yes. Lansing requires every rental property to be registered with Code Compliance, with the exception of an owner-occupied single-family dwelling. The fee schedule effective July 1, 2024 lists a $235 new registration fee, a $55 per building fee for a change of owner, and a base inspection fee of $175 per building for one and two family structures.

When a rental is sold, the buyer takes on the registration, the inspection history and any open citations. Late fees and failure-to-register fees are on the same schedule, so an unregistered rental costs more to sell than a registered one. Ask Code Compliance for the current forms before you list a rental.

Vacant houses face a separate risk. The schedule includes administrative fees for red-tagged properties, emergency board-up and demolition, all of which can be assessed against the parcel.

Closing and after the sale

Your deed goes to whichever of the three county recorders holds the parcel. The state tax on it is $3.75 per $500 of price, a county tax is added on top, and a handful of family transfers escape both. The title company can tell you which line applies.

Within 45 days of closing the buyer reports the sale to Lansing's assessor, and the house's taxable value is rebased for the following year. You have 90 days after moving out to cancel your homestead school-tax exemption.

Weighing an investor's cash offer against a listing comes down to the net figure after taxes, recording costs and any city fees. Before you decide, collect these papers:

  • Your deed and the county named on your tax bill
  • Rental registration and inspection records, if the house was rented
  • Receipts for major repairs
  • A payoff figure from the Treasurer for any open tax bill

A cash buyer takes the house as it stands, including open citations and a rental registration, which can save you the cost of repairs and a long wait for a lender.

Step by step: from offer to keys

A typical Lansing sale moves in a clear order. First, confirm the county on your tax bill, because that county's register of deeds will record the deed. Second, if the house is a rental, call Code Compliance and ask for the current forms and any open citations. Third, pick your route: a listing, a private sale or a cash offer. Fourth, ask the Treasurer for the status of both tax bills so nothing is left unpaid when the title company prorates them. Fifth, at closing, sign the deed and settlement statement and make sure the transfer tax lines match what the title company quoted.

After closing, mark your calendar for the 90-day window to cancel your homestead exemption. The buyer handles the assessor report, but it is smart to confirm with the title company that it was sent. A cash purchase skips the buyer's appraisal and loan approval, and it often skips the repair requests that follow a buyer's inspection. That can matter for an older house where the furnace, porch or basement would otherwise be negotiated line by line, and it gives you a firm closing date to plan your move around.

The county where the parcel sits records it. Lansing spans Ingham, Eaton and Clinton counties, so read the county on your tax bill and ask that county's register of deeds.

When is the last day to pay Lansing winter taxes?

February 14 is the last day to pay winter taxes. Ask the Lansing Treasurer when open bills move to the county.

Do I need to tell the city I sold my house?

The buyer reports the sale to the assessor, and you cancel your homestead exemption within 90 days of moving out.

Selling in Dearborn: the Certificate of Occupancy

Dearborn sellers face one step that most Michigan sellers never see: the city requires a Certificate of Occupancy before a house can close. It comes from a city inspection and is issued in the buyer's name, so the timing has to be planned from the day you decide to sell.

Dearborn is a first-ring suburb in Wayne County, about seven miles west of downtown Detroit, with 105,611 residents in the 2025 estimate. Ford's world headquarters and the River Rouge complex sit here, and many owners live close to a Ford job, a hospital or one of the two colleges. Buyers often start their search with commute time, so a short drive to those places helps a listing.

How the pre-sale inspection works

The seller, the listing agent or a legally appointed power of attorney files a residential inspection request with the city's Economic Development Department and pays the fee with it. City staff then call to set the visit, which takes about 45 minutes. An adult aged 18 or older must be home for the whole inspection.

The inspector checks basic safety and property maintenance against the city's minimum housing standards, then issues a written report. Every item on that report counts as a code violation and has to be fixed and re-inspected. The sequence runs like this:

  • Submit the application and payment.
  • Wait for staff to schedule the inspection.
  • Be present for the walk-through and keep the report.
  • Correct each listed item. The clock is twelve months from the first inspection day.
  • Request a re-inspection and pass it.
  • Email the buyer's name to the city sales address and say whether the buyer will live in the house, so the certificate can be prepared.

A report holds for twelve months, so a house that falls out of contract can be relisted without a second full inspection while that window is open.

Property tax bills and payoffs

Dearborn sends two bills a year, and each carries different taxing bodies. Whichever bill is open at your closing decides what the settlement statement shows.

  • The summer bill is levied July 1 and due September 14. It holds the school tax, the city tax and the county-allocated operating tax. An owner can pay it in three pieces (September 14, November 14, January 14) for a one-time $3 charge.
  • The winter bill is levied December 1 and due February 14. The county's remaining levies and the city's combined sewer overflow debt ride on it, and the whole amount is paid at once.

Before closing, ask the Treasury Division for a written payoff so the closing agent sends the right amount. The cashier counter is at the Dearborn Administrative Center, 16901 Michigan Avenue, open weekdays until half past four. The Assessment Department shares the building and answers value questions at 313-943-2140.

If a bill is unpaid when you list, bring it up with your buyer early. The closing agent can pay it from your proceeds, but only if the payoff figure is on file before the closing date.

State transfer tax and filings after closing

Michigan puts the transfer tax on the seller. On every $500 block of sale value the state takes $3.75 (MCL 207.525), and Wayne County adds its own levy under MCL 207.504, which sets 55 cents per block in counties under two million residents. Ask Wayne County's deed office for the exact county figure before you build a net sheet.

MCL 207.526 carves out some deeds. Dearborn owners most often meet the exemption for a deed between spouses that changes how they hold title, and the one for a land contract whose legal title has not yet passed.

After closing, the buyer notifies the assessor inside 45 days (MCL 211.27a). For the following tax year the taxable value is set at the SEV, and the inflation cap resumes a year later. If you held a principal residence exemption, ask the Dearborn assessor for the form that removes it.

Which selling route fits a house with open inspection items?

A listed sale usually brings the highest price but makes you finish every cited repair before closing. An investor who plans to renovate or rent the house faces the same certificate requirement, and the city asks whether the buyer intends to live there. A private sale lets you and the buyer agree in writing on who pays for corrections, which helps when the inspection list is long.

A long list is the usual reason a Dearborn sale slips. Book the inspection early, settle in writing who handles each correction, and keep the report in your closing file. A cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands can take the repair list off your plate, though the city still wants its inspection and the buyer's name before it issues the certificate.

A sensible order of steps

Start with the inspection request, because everything else waits on the city's calendar. While you wait for the visit, call the Treasury Division for your payoff and ask Wayne County's deed office what the county transfer tax will be. Those two numbers let you work out what you actually keep from a sale.

Once the report arrives, sort the items into cheap fixes you can finish yourself and larger repairs that need a contractor. Keep receipts and the re-inspection result together in one folder. When you have a contract, send the buyer's name to the city sales address and confirm whether the buyer will occupy the house. The closing agent will want the certificate, the tax payoff and the deed ready at the table, and a missing piece is the most common reason a Dearborn closing gets pushed back.

Frequently asked questions

Is a city inspection required before my Dearborn house can close?

Yes. Dearborn will not let a sale close without a Certificate of Occupancy, and the certificate follows a pre-sale inspection. You, your agent or a power of attorney requests the visit, fixes any violations, passes a re-inspection and then emails the buyer's name to city staff.

How long is a Dearborn inspection report valid?

Twelve months, counting from the first inspection. That is also your window to correct every listed violation and pass the re-inspection, so a failed sale does not force a second full inspection if you relist inside it.

When are Dearborn property taxes due?

Summer taxes are due September 14 and winter taxes February 14. The summer bill may be split into payments on September 14, November 14 and January 14. The winter bill has no split option.

Who pays the state transfer tax in a Dearborn sale?

The seller. Michigan makes the grantor liable, at $3.75 for each $500 block of value for the state plus the Wayne County levy. A few deeds are exempt, such as a spouse's deed creating a tenancy by the entireties.

How does a sale change the tax bill?

It usually rises for the buyer. For the following tax year the taxable value is set at the SEV, and the inflation cap resumes a year later. Your own exemption ends once you rescind it with the assessor.

Selling a house in Livonia

Livonia is a large suburb on Detroit's west side, with owners living in 87.2 percent of its housing. That ratio means most sales are ordinary owner-to-buyer transfers, with a smaller group of rentals that fall under a strict city licensing program.

The July 1, 2025 population estimate is 92,603, a 3.1 percent drop from the 2020 base of 95,529. Much of the housing went up in the postwar years, when the city grew quickly after becoming a city in 1950, so gather your permit history before you list. The city issues permits for additions, decks, basement finishing and similar work, and open permits or violations are tracked by the Inspection Department.

Schools and getting around

Most addresses fall in Livonia Public Schools, which runs Franklin, Churchill and Stevenson high schools. A portion of northeast Livonia is served by the Clarenceville School District. Check the district for your exact street before the listing names a school zone.

The mean trip to work is 24.3 minutes, and public bus service is limited, so households here depend on cars. Highway access and garage space are therefore worth mentioning in a listing. Does a Livonia rental need a license before it can be sold?

Livonia licenses and inspects rentals, and a rental may not be occupied without a rental license and a Certificate of Compliance. Licenses renew annually or at title transfer, and inspections happen annually, at a change of tenants or at a change of ownership, whichever comes first.

If you own a rental and plan to sell, take these steps:

  • Give the Inspection Department a copy of the purchase agreement, which lets the city cancel a renewal that was already scheduled.
  • Keep any follow-up inspection already booked so open violations get cleared.
  • Tell the buyers the city will need to inspect if violations remain after title moves.
  • After closing, the new owners take their Property Transfer Affidavit and Homestead Affidavit to the Assessor and then bring copies to the inspectors.

The city applies the state occupancy standard of 225 square feet for the first person and 70 for each additional person, not counting baths or closets. Common rental violations include dryer venting, missing smoke alarms and GFCI outlets, and a furnace carbon monoxide check every three years by a mechanical contractor. Call the Inspection Department at 734-466-2580 for the current fees and wait times, because the lead time can run about a month.

Property tax due dates

The city sends real and personal property tax bills on July 1 and December 1, so a house that closes in between usually has one bill still to be divided between buyer and seller. The summer bill's deadline is September 14. The Treasurer then splits the collections among the city, two school districts (Livonia and Clarenceville), Schoolcraft College, the state education tax, Wayne County, Wayne RESA and the Oakland ISD.

Delinquent real property taxes go to the Wayne County Treasurer. Fees for open permits, violations, vacant or abandoned property registration and Certificate of Occupancy issues never appear in the online tax lookup. Call the Inspection Department about those. Special assessment requests go by email to the Treasurer's office.

Check the city's online property inquiry before closing so your title company can see the tax history for the parcel. If the inquiry shows anything odd, call the Treasurer's office early rather than at the closing table.

How a Livonia deed is recorded and taxed

Livonia sits inside Wayne County, so the Wayne County Register of Deeds handles recording. Before recording, a deed normally needs tax certification from the county treasurer, unless an exemption applies. The register's fee schedule from January 1, 2026 lists $26 per document plus a $4 survey fee where applicable, and service is by appointment.

The state transfer tax is $3.75 for every $500 of the sale price. Wayne County charges its own levy on top, and your title company should quote the two together. Some deeds owe nothing, such as gifts to children and grandchildren.

Two deadlines start at closing. The buyer must report the transfer to the Livonia assessor within 45 days. You must cancel your homestead exemption within 90 days of moving out if you no longer qualify.

A traditional listing fits a Livonia house that shows well, if you can live with weeks of showings. A cash sale suits a house with open violations, a tenant, or deferred repairs. Whichever you choose, collect your deed information, the last tax bills, and any permit paperwork first. If the house was a rental, call the Inspection Department about the purchase agreement before you accept an offer. A cash buyer takes the house as it stands and does not wait on a lender. The title company then arranges the county certification and recording. Compare offers by the net you keep after taxes, recording costs and any repairs.

What to do in the weeks before closing

Begin by asking city hall what is still open on the house. Ask the Inspection Department whether any permits are still open, because a finished deck or basement with no final inspection can slow a sale. Next, check the online tax inquiry for the parcel and confirm the summer and winter bills are paid or ready to be prorated. Then call the Treasurer's office about any special assessment, which is handled by email.

If you rent the house, tell your tenants about the sale and give the buyer the lease terms. Remind the buyer that the city will need to inspect if violations remain after title moves, and that the new owners take their affidavits to the Assessor. On closing day, bring your deed information and an ID, and ask the title company for a settlement statement that lists the recording fee, the survey fee where it applies, and both transfer taxes. Keep copies of everything you sign. A record of your move date also helps when you cancel the homestead exemption, and your agent or title officer can usually supply it.

How many people live in Livonia?

The July 1, 2025 estimate is 92,603 residents. That is down 3.1 percent from the April 2020 base.

Who records a deed for a house in Livonia?

The county register of deeds, after the county treasurer certifies the taxes. Service there is by appointment.

When is the summer tax bill due in Livonia?

Billing goes out July 1 for summer, with a September 14 deadline that rolls to the next business day on weekends and holidays. Winter bills follow on December 1.

Does my Livonia rental need an inspection before I sell it?

Send the Inspection Department the purchase agreement so a scheduled inspection can be cancelled or kept to clear violations. The city inspects rentals at a change of ownership, so call 734-466-2580.

Which school districts serve Livonia?

Livonia Public Schools covers most addresses and operates Franklin, Churchill and Stevenson high schools. Part of northeast Livonia belongs to Clarenceville, so look up your own street.

Choosing the quickest way to sell in Troy

Troy sellers can price a listing to draw several bids, line up a buyer on their own, or accept cash from a buyer who asks for no repairs. Home values in Troy run high for the area, so weeks of prep can earn real money, but cash fits an owner short on time.

Owners' median home value is $420,300 and median household income is $120,045 for 2020 through 2024. Buyers at that price read inspection reports closely. Heavy repairs, an estate or a job move can steer a seller to one offer from a buyer who takes on the work.

  • Agent listing: suits a house in good shape and a seller who can live with inspection and lender timelines.
  • Private sale: possible if you can produce a contract and a deed that the county will accept.
  • Cash offer: fits when speed, privacy or the house's condition outweighs getting the highest price.

The Troy market

In Oakland County, Troy covers 33.45 square miles of land, borders Sterling Heights to the east, and has an estimated 88,733 residents as of mid-2025, up from 87,294 in 2020. Troy incorporated as a city in 1955. In ZIP code 48098 the January average low is 22 degrees Fahrenheit and precipitation totals near 32 inches a year, which is why inspectors check roofs and gutters carefully.

Big Beaver Road anchors the business district, with the Somerset Collection mall and the Oakland Mall nearby. Retail sales reached $4.17 billion in 2022, about $47,709 per resident, so shopping and jobs sit close to most neighborhoods.

School districts in Troy

Seven districts divide Troy. The home district for most addresses is Troy School District, with twelve elementary schools, four middle schools, Troy High and Athens High, plus the International Academy's eastern campus. Elementary buildings inside the city also belong to Avondale, Birmingham and Warren Consolidated, while Bloomfield Hills, Royal Oak and Lamphere cover small areas.

Neighbors may attend different districts, so put the district in your listing, and verify any address close to a boundary.

Assessments and tax bills

Troy's assessor sets assessed value at half of market value. That office also handles the Principal Residence Exemption and the Property Transfer Affidavit.

  • Summer bill: goes out July 1 and is clear of penalty through September 1. A 4% charge follows, with half a percent monthly starting October 1.
  • Winter bill: goes out December 1 and is clear through February 14, followed by 3%.
  • On March 1, open current-year balances shift to the Oakland County Treasurer at 248.858.0611, option 7.

Troy collects for seven school districts plus the county, Oakland Schools, Macomb Intermediate and several county authorities. School levies change with the district and with principal-residence status, so look-alike houses can get different bills. An owner who is 62 or older or disabled, with income at or under $40,000, can apply through September 15 to defer payment to April 30.

A sale lifts the cap on the buyer's taxable value starting the next calendar year. Prorations are set by contract, and call the Treasurer's Office at 248.524.3333 to learn what is due on a given date. The Assessor, Clerk and Treasurer all work out of City Hall at 500 W. Big Beaver Road, which usually lets you finish records and tax errands in one visit.

Transfer tax and the Oakland County Register of Deeds

State law puts the transfer tax on the seller, payable within 15 days after the deed is delivered (MCL 207.523). The state's piece is $3.75 for every $500 (MCL 207.525), and the county's piece is 55 cents per $500 for counties under 2,000,000 residents (MCL 207.504). Check the Oakland County figure with the register before you close.

Reach the Register of Deeds at 248-858-0597 or deeds@oaklandcountymi.gov on weekdays; the counter opens at 8:30 a.m. Deeds, mortgages and foreclosure records are filed there, and the Super Index can retrieve recorded documents dating to January 1, 1964.

MCL 207.526 exempts gifts to children and grandchildren, foreclosure deeds and court orders that state no price. The deed itself has to cite the exemption.

Yard and property rules to settle before showings

Troy's Code Enforcement office posts the complaints it fields most. A single walk around the property before the first showing can save you a violation notice mid-listing.

  • Grass and weeds must stay below 8 inches between May 1 and October 31, including the strip to the road.
  • Sidewalk snow over 2 inches and any ice must be cleared within 24 hours of a storm.
  • Vehicles kept on private land must carry current plates and run, and RVs cannot sit on the street.
  • Temporary signs are allowed on private property, while signs in the public right-of-way are removed.
  • Put bins out only after 5 p.m. the evening before pickup, and trim branches over sidewalks up to 8 feet.

Put open house and yard signs on your own lot only. Two more rules matter to some sellers: one commercial pickup or cargo van may sit on private property in a one-family district, and home businesses are allowed in one- and two-family districts under conditions, so a buyer planning to work from the house should call Code Enforcement first.

Putting a Troy sale together

Begin with taxes: find out from the Treasurer's Office where your bill stands and how proration would work on your planned closing date. Check the yard against the list above. Take offers in writing, and have each bidder name a closing date and say who covers transfer tax. A cash buyer has no lender appraisal holding things up, so timing depends mostly on title work and the deed. After you accept, the title company drafts the deed, confirms the transfer tax and sends it to the Register of Deeds.

Hand the title company your payoff letter, a recent tax bill and permit records, and mention right away if the deed qualifies for an exemption. A buyer who intends to rent the house or run a business from it should talk to Code Enforcement before closing. Request a written closing statement from the title company showing the tax proration, the transfer tax and the recording fee, and compare every line to your contract before you sign. If anything looks off, raise it with the title company before closing day, since fixing a figure afterward takes longer.

Frequently asked questions

What is a typical Troy home worth?

Owner-occupied homes had a median value of $420,300 in 2020 to 2024, though age, lot and district move individual prices.

When do Troy tax bills come due?

You can pay the summer bill through September 1 and the winter bill through February 14. Balances still open on March 1 move to Oakland County.

Do Troy taxes reset after I sell?

For the buyer they can. A transfer of ownership lifts the cap on taxable value the following calendar year.

Which school district is a Troy house in?

Troy School District covers most houses. Avondale, Birmingham, Bloomfield Hills, Lamphere, Royal Oak and Warren Consolidated each serve some areas.

Where is a Troy deed recorded?

At the Oakland County Register of Deeds, 248-858-0597. The deed pays transfer tax unless it names an exemption.

Selling a house in Farmington Hills

Homes here carry some of the highest values in Oakland County, so a hurried sale rarely fails for lack of buyers. It stalls on condition, paperwork and timing. Farmington Hills spreads across roughly 33 square miles, about 22 miles northwest of downtown Detroit, and its 2020 Census count of 83,986 made it the county's second-largest community.

An owner can hire an agent, sell privately, or hand the keys to a cash purchaser who takes the house as it stands. Each path trades repair cost, showing effort and waiting time differently.

Housing stock and what buyers expect

The city was incorporated in 1973 from two small villages and the rest of the township, and it grew quickly through the middle of the twentieth century. The houses on your street may belong to very different eras. A subdivision laid out in the 1960s and a newer estate lot can sit a few minutes apart and attract unlike buyers. The count of housing units, 37,382 in 2020 with 5.4% vacant, shows a built-out city where almost every sale is a resale.

  • Houses from the early decades of the boom can need new roofs, windows and furnaces before a lender-financed buyer will close.
  • Condominium owners should gather the association's governing documents early, since buyers and lenders request them.
  • Estate-style homes are priced against recent nearby sales, so a pre-listing appraisal is worth considering.

City rules: rentals and permits

Single-family rentals must be registered under a mandatory program, and each one is inspected every third year for exterior condition, fire safety, egress, structural and electrical soundness, pests and trash. If tenants occupy the house you plan to sell, ask the Planning and Community Development office how a change of owner affects the registration and certificate of compliance.

Permit rules matter just as much. A building permit is needed for roofing, siding, window and exterior door replacement, basement finishing, decks and pools, and trade permits cover water heaters, furnaces, air conditioning and sump pumps. A homeowner may pull permits personally only when the person holds title, lives in the home and treats it as the primary residence. The Building Division answers at (248) 871-2450, and residential fence questions go to Zoning at (248) 871-2520.

  • Before listing, ask the Building Division whether any permit on the address is still open.
  • Patios, playground equipment and backboards need no building permit but must satisfy zoning.
  • Poured concrete without footings falls under the Engineering Department's right-of-way rules, reachable at (248) 871-2560.

Tax calendar and closing

Farmington Hills mails its summer bill June 30 and its winter bill November 30. Summer taxes may be paid July 1 through August 31, winter taxes from December 1 to mid-February, and the city adds a 4% penalty after each window. Balances that remain open at the city's March deadline pass to the Oakland County Treasurer. The city's Treasury and Assessing offices answer at 248-871-2480 and 248-871-2470.

Owners who live in the house and are at least 62, disabled, or an eligible veteran or surviving spouse may apply to defer summer taxes if household income is under a set limit. The form sets that limit at $40,000. The title company prorates the current bill between you and the buyer, and a payoff letter from Treasury confirms nothing from a prior year remains.

Transfer tax and after-sale filings

Michigan levies a county tax of 55 cents and a state tax of $3.75 on every $500 of price, a rate pair set out in MCL 207.504 and 207.525. Sellers owe both, and the settlement statement shows the total.

After closing, the buyer reports the sale to the city assessor within 45 days. Taxable value then resets to the state equalized value (MCL 211.27a), which is why a buyer's first full tax bill can look steep beside the seller's capped one.

Schools and commuting routes

Nearly all of the city belongs to Farmington Public Schools. Small corners fall within Clarenceville and Walled Lake Consolidated. North Farmington High School and Farmington Central High School operate within the city limits.

Drivers rely on M-5, I-696 and I-275 along with Orchard Lake Road and 12 Mile Road, and SMART runs the local buses. Naming the correct district and the nearest freeway ramp in your listing answers the questions most buyers ask first.

When an as-is cash sale beats a listing

A full listing pays off when the house is updated, you can keep it show-ready and a few months of carrying cost is acceptable. A direct as-is sale is stronger when a roof, mechanicals or an estate cleanout stand between you and a market-ready home, or when a relocation date is fixed.

  • Registered rentals with a current certificate may attract landlords looking for ready income.
  • Houses with open permits may be better sold as-is than corrected under deadline.
  • Sellers who still live in the house can compare a cash closing date against a financed buyer's timeline.

Ask for any offer in writing, and compare net proceeds after transfer tax, prorated taxes and credits.

A short checklist before you list

Begin with the Building Division call about open permits, since an unfinished deck or furnace swap is easy to close out when you catch it early and awkward when a buyer's inspector finds it. If you rent the house, ask Planning and Community Development for the certificate of compliance history, and keep it with your lease. Condominium sellers should request the association papers now.

Next, call Treasury for a payoff letter and Assessing for the parcel's current numbers. Then decide how much work you want to take on. Some owners finish small repairs and list. Others skip the work, accept an as-is offer, and let the closing agent handle prorations and the transfer tax from the sale price. Either way, ask for the closing date in writing so the tax calendar and your move line up.

Frequently asked questions

Will open permits block my sale?

They may, since lenders and buyers' inspectors can ask for proof that finished work was permitted. The Building Division at (248) 871-2450 can tell you whether any permit on your address remains open.

Who is responsible for the Michigan transfer tax?

The seller, under the state act. The state charges $3.75 per $500 of price and the county adds 55 cents, and the county treasurer collects it after the deed is delivered.

My tenant rents the house. Does the city inspection follow the house to the new owner?

Ask Planning and Community Development. The city registers single-family rentals and inspects them every three years, so the buyer will want the certificate of compliance history.

Which dates matter for tax payments?

Summer bills are payable July 1 through August 31 and winter bills from December 1 to mid-February. A 4% penalty follows each window, and unpaid balances go to the Oakland County Treasurer.

Why would the new owner's tax bill be higher than mine?

A sale resets taxable value to the state equalized value in the following year. Your bill reflected annual caps, while the buyer's starts from the full figure. Assessing at 248-871-2470 can quote the parcel's numbers.

The first thing to know about selling in Westland

Before anything else, a Westland seller needs a Certificate of Approval from the city. Every house that is sold or transferred must have one before the residential sale closes, so the certificate sets the pace for the whole deal. The Building Division handles it, and the seller normally opens the file.

Westland is in Wayne County, roughly 18 miles west of downtown Detroit. Deeds for Westland houses go to the Wayne County Register of Deeds, whose appointment system, fees and tax-certification step differ from those in Macomb or Kent counties.

The Westland market

Westland formed as a city on May 16, 1966, out of Nankin Township, and now spans 20.4 square miles. Ford Road (M-153) crosses central Westland, and Wayne County's Hines Park lies along the northern edge. Garbage goes out weekly in the black bin, and the blue recycling bin is picked up every second week.

The city has 82,333 people as of July 1, 2025, which is 3.6 percent less than the 2020 base of 85,409. The 2020 count found 39,633 housing units, 4.9 percent of them empty, and 35,932 households of 2.30 people apiece between 2020 and 2024.

Owners live in only 61.3 percent of Westland homes, a smaller share than in many Michigan suburbs, which is one reason the city's rental rules draw attention. Homes lived in by their owners have a median value of $184,600. Renters pay $1,158 a month at the median, and household income has a median of $62,076. Owners with a mortgage pay $1,360 a month at the median.

School districts serving Westland addresses

The Wayne-Westland Community School District covers most of the city. John Glenn High School serves central Westland and part of the north, and some southern blocks feed Wayne Memorial High School in the city of Wayne. The far northern edge belongs to Livonia Public Schools, whose Churchill and Franklin high schools take those students.

Corners of southeastern Westland are divided between Romulus Community Schools and the Taylor School District, after the Inkster district was dissolved. Assignments can change within a block, so ask the district about the exact address and pass the answer to the buyer.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Westland house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How the Westland Certificate of Approval works

The seller sends the Building Division (36300 Warren Road, phone 734-467-3210, open weekdays 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.) a Home Sale or Transfer application. An inspector then walks the house against the property maintenance code. Inspections can be booked online, by email to building@cityofwestland.com, by phone or at the counter.

  • A mechanical contractor registered with Westland tests the furnace or boiler and signs the city's own certification form.
  • If the home has a fireplace, a chimney contractor files a safety inspection report as well.
  • A seller who completes the process receives a certificate that stays valid for six months.
  • A seller who stops short leaves a second path: the buyer pays $80 for an Approval Letter to Close, files a Remaining Violations Disclosure Form along with the signed purchase agreement, and then gets ninety days to fix the items and book the final inspection.

That second path can suit an as-is cash purchase, because the closing proceeds with the open items and the repairs shift to the buyer. The furnace or boiler certification must be on file before final approval is granted.

Plan the order of work this way: book the inspection first, line up the furnace and chimney reports, and decide early whether you will finish repairs yourself or let the buyer take the Approval Letter route. Bring permit numbers for any past work to the visit, and keep the certificate with your sale papers once it is issued.

Open permits and rentals

The Building Division issues the permits that homeowners most often skip: re-roofing, decks, fences, fireplaces, garages, pools, kitchen expansions and basement finishing all need one, and electrical, plumbing and heating work each take a separate trade permit. A housing inspector walking the house for the Certificate of Approval is likely to ask about any of that work, so gather permit numbers and final approvals before the visit.

Westland also runs a rental program, with a Rental Registration Application on the Building Division's forms list. An owner selling a tenant-occupied house should ask the Building Division at 734-467-3210 how the registration and the sale certificate interact, and whether the rental registration is current before the house goes under contract.

The Planning and Building Department also lists a Temporary Certificate of Occupancy request form, a separate route used while work is still unfinished. Ask the department whether that form applies to your situation before you promise a buyer a closing date.

City and county charges on a Westland sale

The city's fee varies with building type. On the county side, recording a deed costs $26 plus a $4 state survey fee, under a schedule that took effect January 1, 2026. Deeds and land contracts also need Wayne County treasurer certification unless an exemption applies.

City certificate, multi-family building$900

State transfer tax$3.75 for each $500 of consideration

Wayne County restates the combined rate as $8.60 per $1,000, payable at the recording counter. For property tax amounts and due dates, call the Westland Finance Department before closing.
